transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Yeah, thanks. I guess what finally pushed me to come in is… I can’t seem to keep all the moving parts organized anymore. Like, at work I’ve got patent notes in one place, workshop prep somewhere else, gallery deadlines—well, that’s a side project, but still—and then team decisions that need follow-up, and somehow I end up doing whatever is loudest right in front of me instead of the thing that actually matters most.

It’s frustrating because I’m not trying to drop things. I’ll start the day thinking I know what needs to happen, and then an email or a message or some urgent-looking thing pulls me sideways, and by the end I’ve touched six things but finished the wrong one. That’s basically why I’m here.
Thinking back, would you say you've struggled with this kind of distractibility and trouble prioritizing since you were a child, or is this really a new pattern that started more recently?

No, it definitely wasn’t just recent. I mean, I can make it sound like it’s because work got more complicated, and it has, but looking back… yeah, this was there when I was a kid too.

In grade school, teachers would write stuff like I was bright, but I daydreamed a lot. And I remember—well, my mom kept some of those report cards for years, in this big folder with school pictures and random certificates—but the comments were always kind of the same. I’d do the assignment and then somehow not turn it in, or I’d lose the homework folder before it made it back to school.

So, yeah, long before I was a teenager, that pattern was already there.
Besides the trouble organizing and staying focused, do you also notice things like feeling restless, fidgety, or having trouble sitting still, or acting impulsively without thinking things through?

Yeah, I do get restless, especially on long design calls. It’s like there’s this pressure building up in my body to move, even if I’m trying to look like I’m paying attention. I’ll pace around my office, or move from one chair to another, or kind of shift around a lot.

It’s funny, I actually set up my office thinking it would make me more focused—good chair, second chair by the window, standing desk mat I barely use correctly—but on those calls I end up rotating around the room like that’s somehow part of the process. So yes, I wouldn’t say I’m bouncing off the walls, but sitting still for a long meeting can be really hard.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others, blurting out responses before they finish speaking, or making quick decisions without fully thinking them through?

Um… I’m not sure that’s the main thing for me. I don’t think of myself as someone who’s constantly cutting people off, at least not in a way people have pointed out.

I mean, in meetings I’ll sometimes want to jump in because the conversation is moving fast, and if I don’t say the thought then it sort of… anyway, that’s probably not what you’re asking. I try pretty hard to wait my turn, especially at work, because those conversations can get messy quickly.

Quick decisions… I don’t know. I can overthink things too, so I wouldn’t say I’m always impulsive. I guess I’d need an example of what you mean.
Does this kind of disorganization and distractibility also cause problems for you outside of work—like at home, in relationships, or managing personal responsibilities?

Yeah, I mean… the place it’s been most obvious, or at least most embarrassing, is work. I know you asked outside of work, and I’m trying to think about that, but the thing that keeps coming to mind is that it’s started affecting how people see me professionally.

Like, I missed a checkpoint for a patent filing—not the final filing, but one of those internal steps where you’re supposed to have things lined up—and that was… not great. And then there was this architecture review that went badly. It was a difficult one anyway, lots of moving pieces, but I wasn’t on top of it the way I should’ve been, and afterward I got the sense that some collaborators were questioning whether I could really lead the larger project.

So, I guess the short answer is: yes, it causes real problems, but the biggest damage I can point to is my work reputation. That’s the part that’s been hard to ignore.

Can you give me a specific example of how this disorganization or distractibility has caused a problem at home or in your personal life—like forgetting bills, appointments, or commitments to family or friends?

Yeah… I’m trying to think of a clean home example, like a bill or a dentist appointment, but honestly the pattern shows up more as everything bleeding together.

What finally pushed me to come in is that I can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. I’ve got patent notes in one place, workshop prep in another, gallery deadlines—my partner is involved in some of that world too, so it sort of spills into personal life—and then team decisions sitting in Slack or email or wherever. And instead of doing the thing that actually matters next, I end up starting whatever is loudest or most urgent-feeling in the moment.

So at home it’s less like, “I forgot one specific bill,” and more like I’m surrounded by half-sorted notes and reminders and I can’t make a sane plan out of it. Then something personal gets neglected because I spent the evening chasing the wrong task.

Can you think of a specific recent example, outside of work, where this distractibility or disorganization caused a problem—like something with your partner, a household task, or a personal commitment that got missed or messed up?

Yeah… I’m trying to pin down one specific thing, and I keep coming back to the same mess, basically. Like at home, it’s not just “I forgot to take out the trash” or something simple. It’s that I’ll have all these separate threads—patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, decisions from the team—and they’re all scattered in different places.

And then in the evening I’ll sit down meaning to handle, say, something related to the gallery or something my partner was expecting me to follow up on, but I’ll notice some other note or message that feels more urgent, and suddenly I’m reorganizing that instead. Or half-reorganizing it, really. Then the actual thing that mattered doesn’t get done.

So the problem is less one missed appointment and more that I can’t seem to organize the moving parts anymore. I end up doing whatever is loudest in front of me, not what actually matters, and then it spills into home stuff.

Can you recall one specific instance—like forgetting a plan with your partner, missing a personal deadline, or failing to follow through on a household responsibility—where this disorganization actually caused a real consequence at home, separate from work?

I know you’re asking for one clean example, and I’m… annoyingly, I’m still thinking in piles rather than one event.

The real thing is that I can’t organize the moving parts anymore. I’ll have patent notes over here, workshop prep somewhere else, gallery deadlines in another place, and team decisions buried in messages. And then at home, when I’m supposed to follow through on something that actually matters, I’ll start with whatever feels loudest in front of me instead.

So the consequence is that the important thing gets pushed aside—not because I don’t care, but because I never get the pieces sorted into a real plan. That’s honestly what pushed me to come in. It’s like I’m constantly reacting to the nearest thread instead of doing the thing I actually meant to do.

Let's try a different angle: has your partner ever told you they were frustrated, hurt, or upset because you forgot something you'd promised to do for them—regardless of whether you can recall the exact details right now?

Yeah, I mean… yes, she has been frustrated. I’m not sure I can give you the exact quote or the one perfect incident, but the pattern is there.

It’s usually not that I don’t want to do the thing for her. It’s more like I’ve got all these moving pieces in my head and in different places—patent notes, workshop stuff, gallery deadlines, team decisions—and then I sit down intending to follow through on something that matters, and I get pulled into whatever feels loudest right then.

And then later it turns out the thing she needed from me was the thing I didn’t do. So… yes, she gets upset about that. It’s embarrassing, because from the outside it just looks like I didn’t care or didn’t listen, but inside it feels like I can’t get the pieces into an order that makes sense.

He also endorses hyperactive-restless symptoms (pacing, shifting seats, inner restlessness during meetings) but denies significant impulsivity (interrupting, blurting, rash decisions). Symptoms cause clear functional impairment at work (missed patent filing checkpoint, poor performance in architecture review, damaged professional reputation) and cause relational friction at home (partner's frustration over unmet commitments), though he struggles to name a single discrete home incident, describing instead a pervasive pattern of task-switching and incomplete follow-through. The combination of chronic inattentive symptoms with prominent hyperactive-restless features, childhood onset, and cross-situational impairment supports ADHD, combined presentation, best captured by F90.0 given ICD-10 conventions bundling combined hyperactive-inattentive ADHD into F90.0 (Hyperkinetic disorder, disturbance of activity and attention).
